title: CRVS Data Quality & Health Resource Allocation
text:
Does the quality of South Africa’s civil registration and vital statistics (CRVS) data distort how health budgets are allocated across programmes? This project builds a real, verifiable data pipeline to investigate that question — it does not assume the answer.
This is an internal working project, not a finished result. Every chapter below states plainly what is confirmed vs. still open. This site publishes the rendered chapters only; research code, underlying dataset files, and internal source registers remain local. Interactive tables and charts contain their displayed values, and links to original public sources are retained.









Overview


Research question, hypothesis, and project status at a glance.










Budget Panel


Explore the real provincial Health-department budget (EPRE 2024-25), by province, programme, and year.










Descriptive Statistics


Real budget composition figures for both provincial (EPRE) and national (ENE) data, browsable by tab instead of private markdown notes.










Programme Crosswalk & Data Quality


How raw provincial programme-name spelling variants were audited and corrected.










Citation Trail


Which known burden-of-disease data sources are cited in real National DoH strategic documents.










Plan & Open Questions


Working plan status and open design questions (from docs/PLAN.md).

A conceptual, introductory abstract for CPHIA — not a results abstract.










Cross-Country Landscape


What evidence informs national health budgets and strategic plans, compared across D4H countries.

A cross-country citation-landscape abstract across 8 D4H countries, mapping which evidence informs national health policy and budgets.

title: Descriptive Statistics
text:
Framing options for the abstract






Tip



This chapter is the ingredients pantry, not a locked-in argument. Every table, chart, and “so what” above is a raw fact this project can draw on. The titles and questions below are draft framing options for turning some subset of these ingredients into the CPHIA abstract (or a future paper) — none are decided; treat this as a menu to choose from (and combine), not a commitment.



Alternative titles to consider
Current working title (06-cphia-abstract.qmd): “Are African health budgets calibrated to health data quality? A pipeline for auditing civil registration and vital statistics (CRVS) data quality against provincial health budget allocation in South Africa” — the CRVS/data-quality framing. Alternatives grounded in specific findings above:

“Does population size predict health budget allocation? A province-level check against South Africa’s 2022 Census” — narrower, population-vs-budget-ratio-only framing (see Population vs. budget allocation above); easiest to defend since it needs no burden-of-disease data at all, but says nothing about disease-specific need.
“When one disease colonises a programme: HIV/AIDS’s rising share of South Africa’s national Communicable and Non-communicable Diseases budget, 2021-2025” — built on the CNCD subprogramme-composition trend (~76% to ~99%, see CNCD subprogramme composition over time above); a sharper, more provocative framing but narrower in scope than the CRVS argument.
“The vanishing 0.3%: what’s left for non-HIV/TB/maternal-child disease programming in South Africa’s national health budget” — built on the non-HIV/TB/MCWH ~0.28%-of-Vote-18 finding (see Genuinely non-HIV/TB/MCWH disease spending within CNCD above); punchy and concrete, but a single-number headline risks inviting “is that actually a problem?” pushback without the burden-of-disease comparison this project doesn’t yet have.
“Budgeted for what we can count: how South Africa’s health planning documents cite (and don’t cite) burden-of-disease evidence” — citation-trail-led framing (see the Citation Trail chapter); leads with the evidence-use finding rather than the budget-allocation finding, positioning this as a data-quality/evidence-use paper first and a budget paper second.
“What would it take to know if South Africa’s health budget is enough? A descriptive audit of data, budget, and the missing burden-of-disease comparison” — the most honest-about-limitations option; frames the whole project as scoping/diagnostic work rather than a completed funding-gap finding, which may suit a conceptual/ introductory abstract better than a sharper, single-number title would.



Varying questions to consider
Different research-question framings this same dataset can support — useful for deciding which “so what” to lead with in the abstract’s Results/Conclusion, independent of the title chosen above:

Allocation-vs-population: does provincial Health budget allocation track population size, and which provinces sit furthest from parity? (Answerable now, no burden-of-disease data needed — see Population vs. budget allocation above.)
Allocation-vs-burden (the CRVS framing): is health budget allocation calibrated to burden-of-disease evidence, or only to registered/official statistics? (Currently blocked — needs the Stats SA/NCoDV/GBD funding-gap comparison, see the Plan & Open Questions chapter.)
Programme crowding-out: has HIV/AIDS+STIs’ rising share of the CNCD programme actually crowded out other communicable/ non-communicable disease spending over time, or has the CNCD programme simply grown enough that other subprogrammes’ absolute rand hasn’t shrunk even as their share has? (Answerable now from ENE data; the current chapter only shows share, not the absolute-rand trend for other subprogrammes — a real, addressable gap.)
Evidence-use, not allocation: independent of whether the budget is “right,” which data sources do South Africa’s own planning documents actually cite as evidence — and is that mix shifting away from specific, checkable products toward vaguer, harder-to-audit citations over time? (See the Citation Trail chapter’s Stats SA publication-theme-over-time finding.)
Domestic vs. donor framing: how much of South Africa’s HIV/TB response is even visible in domestic budget data (EPRE/ENE) at all, given PEPFAR/Global Fund financing sits structurally outside it? (See Funded by the local fiscus or foreign aid? above — currently only answerable as a floor, not an exact split.)
Planning-vs-execution: independent of whether the planned budget is calibrated to anything, does the province actually spend what it budgets? (Currently unanswerable — see Budget credibility above; would need an additional EPRE vintage with overlapping Main-appropriation and Audited-Outcome years.)

None of these are mutually exclusive — the current abstract draft already leans on a version of (2) and (4) together. Picking a primary question should probably come before finalising the title, not after.

title: Descriptive Statistics
text:
Methodology, limitations & traceability
Provincial (EPRE): totals use Main appropriation only (FY2023-FY2024); programme names are harmonised via apply_programme_crosswalk() (whitespace/spelling normalisation only — see data/crosswalks/programme_name_variants_2024_25.csv); the HIV/AIDS+TB figures are a text-match on subprogramme labels, not an audited HIV/TB programme classification, so a differently worded subprogramme could be missed. The population-adjusted allocation ratio uses real Census 2022 province population shares (SA_PROVINCE_POPULATION_CENSUS2022, R/constants.R) against total population only — no age-structure, disease-burden, or medical-scheme-coverage adjustment, so it is a first screening check, not a resource-allocation-formula critique. Source: fetch_vulekamali() (R/fetch_vulekamali.R); summary functions in R/describe_budget_lines.R (incl. summarise_population_adjusted_allocation()); runner Rscript scripts/run_budget_descriptive_stats.R (writes data/processed/budget_population_comparison.csv among others); tests in tests/testthat/test-describe_budget_lines.R.
National (ENE): the 2021/22-2022/23 “Communicable Diseases” spike is a plausible but not independently confirmed COVID-19 booking effect. Only 2024/25-2027/28 are available for the CNCD-share-of-vote comparison (the vote-wide total sheet only covers those years). Source: fetch_national_ene_health() (R/fetch_national_ene.R); analysis in R/analyse_disease_programme_allocation.R; runner Rscript scripts/run_national_disease_allocation.R; tests in tests/testthat/test-fetch_national_ene.R and tests/testthat/test-analyse_disease_programme_allocation.R.
All CSVs behind this chapter are real and re-derivable from the scripts above — nothing here is estimated or invented.

title: IHEA World Congress Abstract (Draft)
text:
Abstract
Background. Multiple factors influence the decision made for health strategy and budgets. A measurable factor is the evidence cited in national strategic plans, policies and budget documents. This study aims to systematically map and analyze these citations across multiple countries to describe the evidence in shaping health policy and potentially resource allocation.
Objectives. To describe, across South Africa, Zambia, Rwanda, Thailand, Morocco, Uganda, India, and Kenya, which categories of evidence are cited in each country’s national health strategic plans, policies, and budget documents.
Methods. Publicly available national-level documents (2011-2025) were identified by targeted search and individually verified (HTTP status, content type, title-page confirmation). 52 documents were registered: South Africa (9, including 3 provincial Annual Performance Plans), India (11), Morocco (7), Rwanda (6), Uganda (6), Kenya (5), Thailand (4), and Zambia (4). Citations were extracted programmatically and classified into a evidence-category taxonomy, with country-scoped pattern matching to prevent acronym collisions across countries (e.g. “DHS” denotes a district health system in Thailand but a Demographic and Health Survey elsewhere). Each country’s own routine health-information system (e.g. DHIS, KHIS, HMIS) was tracked separately from evidence citations throughout.
Results. The 52 documents yielded 1,966 citation matches: 1,490 to evidence sources and 476 to routine health-information systems. Population-based estimates were the single most-cited evidence category in every country (962/1,490, 65%). National vital statistics were cited in 6 of 8 countries (291 citations, ), absent from Uganda and Morocco. The Global Burden of Disease study was cited in 5 of 8 countries (South Africa and Kenya, 11 citations each; Rwanda, Uganda, and Zambia, 1 each), absent from Thailand, Morocco, and India. Only South Africa cited a domestically-produced burden-of-disease estimate distinct from the global study. A named local epidemiological model appeared in 3 of 8 countries, each for that country’s own HIV response (South Africa, Zambia, Uganda). Verbal autopsy was cited in 4 of 8 countries (1-7 citations each). A named local disease-surveillance system (e.g. Integrated Disease Surveillance and Response) was cited in 5 of 8 countries (107 citations). HDSS infrastructure was cited in only 1 of 8 countries (Kenya), despite verified HDSS research sites in several sampled countries.
Conclusion. Population-based survey and census data dominate the evidence cited in documents that frame national health policy and budgets across all 8 countries, while global burden-of-disease estimates, domestic corrected-burden studies, verbal autopsy, and HDSS infrastructure are cited unevenly and, in most countries, rarely or not at all.
This citation landscape identifies where to target investment in strengthening evidence systems — correcting registered data, building domestic burden-of-disease estimates, extending demographic surveillance and verbal autopsy coverage — in each country. The next step is to establish how far these cited evidence sources actually influence the proportioning of finite health budgets, and whether known data-quality gaps are reflected in how funds are apportioned across programmes.

title: IHEA World Congress Abstract (Draft)
section: Challenging views (critical appraisal, not part of the submission)
text:
Challenging views (critical appraisal, not part of the submission)
A critical reading of this abstract’s own logic, included for honesty rather than resolved:

Citation is not use. A document citing a data source does not establish that the source informed the actual decision, and a source’s absence from a planning document does not establish that it was ignored — it may simply not be the kind of document where that evidence is normally cited. The central premise, that counting citations reveals “what evidence informs policy,” conflates textual reference with decision influence.
Heterogeneous document types inflate apparent differences. Pooling raw counts across an 11-page policy brief, an 1,143-page budget book, and a 650-page statistical profile treats units of very different length and genre as comparable observations; a country’s citation share may track document volume and type mix more than any underlying difference in evidence culture.
Sample depth varies nearly three-fold across countries (4 documents for Thailand/Zambia vs. 11 for India), so cross-country percentage comparisons carry very different amounts of noise per country — a genuinely common citation type can look categorically “absent” in a thin sample purely by chance.
The method cannot detect what it wasn’t built to look for. Pattern coverage was built inductively, country by country, from the documents at hand; a true citation phrased in wording the patterns don’t anticipate is invisible to this pipeline. “Zero citations” is reported identically whether the evidence is genuinely absent or merely phrased outside the known pattern set — the Results cannot distinguish these two cases.
The taxonomy was derived from the same corpus it classifies. Evidence categories were defined inductively from what these documents actually contained, then used to describe what these documents contain — a degree of circularity worth naming rather than presenting as an independently validated instrument.
The recommendation outruns the evidence. A low citation count for a category (e.g. HDSS, domestic burden estimates) is consistent with at least three different explanations — genuine absence of that evidence product in-country, its presence but citation elsewhere (academic literature, not planning documents), or a pattern-coverage gap in this study — and this abstract cannot adjudicate between them, yet the Conclusion still recommends targeting investment as if absence were the only explanation.
The proposed next step assumes its own premise. Testing whether citation practice predicts budget apportionment presupposes that citation practice is diagnostically relevant to budget decisions at all; apportionment may instead follow political and historical path-dependency largely independent of what evidence a planning document cites, in which case a null result there would say nothing about data quality — only about this one causal pathway.

text:
Abstract

We mapped which categories of population-health evidence — census and survey data, civil registration and vital statistics, demographic surveillance, verbal autopsy, global and domestic burden-of-disease estimates, country-specific epidemiological models, and local disease-surveillance systems — are cited in the national health planning and budget documents of eight countries in the Bloomberg Philanthropies Data for Health (D4H) Initiative, using one consistent, auditable classification method.
Objectives. To describe, across South Africa, Zambia, Rwanda, Thailand, Morocco, Uganda, India, and Kenya, which categories of population-health evidence are cited in each country’s national health strategic plans, policies, annual performance and statistical reports, and health or national budget documents.
Methods. Publicly available national-level documents (2011-2025) were identified by targeted search and individually verified (HTTP status, content type, title-page confirmation). 52 documents were registered: South Africa (9, including 3 provincial Annual Performance Plans), India (11), Morocco (7), Rwanda (6), Uganda (6), Kenya (5), Thailand (4), and Zambia (4). Citations were extracted programmatically and classified into a unified evidence-category taxonomy, with country-scoped pattern matching to prevent acronym collisions across countries (e.g. “DHS” denotes a district health system in Thailand but a Demographic and Health Survey elsewhere). A named local epidemiological model appeared in 3 of 8 countries, each for that country’s own HIV response (South Africa, Zambia, Uganda). Verbal autopsy was cited in 4 of 8 countries (1-7 citations each). A named local disease-surveillance system (e.g. Integrated Disease Surveillance and Response) was cited in 5 of 8 countries (107 citations) — a citation type with no equivalent in prior burden-of-disease citation frameworks. HDSS infrastructure was cited in only 1 of 8 countries (Kenya), despite verified HDSS research sites in several sampled countries.
Conclusion. Population-based survey and census data dominate the evidence cited in documents that frame national health policy and budgets across all 8 countries, while global burden-of-disease estimates, domestic corrected-burden studies, verbal autopsy, and HDSS infrastructure are cited unevenly and, in most countries, rarely or not at all. title: CPHIA Conference Abstract (Draft)
text:
Note



Status: draft, conceptual/introductory abstract — grounded only in confirmed facts from docs/KNOWLEDGE.md and the working plan in docs/PLAN.md. This is not a results abstract: the funding-gap analysis has not been run yet (see the Plan & Open Questions chapter, steps 2-3, “not yet built”). The abstract below introduces the research question and the data infrastructure built so far — every number it cites is drawn from one of the larger analysis chapters linked inline below and in the Traceability note at the end — it does not report a tested hypothesis.
Editorial pass (2026-09-24), against your own handwritten draft: broadened the Background opening to the proportional-funding framing from your draft; Methods now discloses AI-assisted code generation (generic wording — “AI-assisted extraction pipeline”, no specific product/model named — since you weren’t available to confirm; revert to “programmatic text search” with no AI mention, or name the specific tool, if you’d rather) and mentions the ministry’s own routine systems (DHIS/TIER.net/EDRWeb) as a fourth tracked category, matching your draft’s Methods list; Conclusion now names NCDs and violence/injury-related spending explicitly as the concrete next funding-gap application, per your Discussion paragraph.
Follow-up (2026-09-24, later same day): challenged the Background’s opening premise (“health spending is positively associated with health outcomes”, stated as unqualified fact with no citation) — this contradicts docs/KNOWLEDGE.md’s own framing that the spending-outcomes link is a separately-tested, contested empirical question, and that this project’s actual contribution sits upstream of it (whether spending is calibrated to burden at all, regardless of whether spending is effective). Background reworded to open on that upstream framing instead of asserting the contested premise.
Second follow-up (2026-09-24, later still): you flagged that you no longer fully endorse the normative claim that spending should track disease burden in strict proportion, while still standing behind the epistemic claim that corrected/adjusted burden estimates beat raw registered counts as inputs to whatever allocation rule is actually used. Background reworded again to decouple these two claims explicitly: proportionality-to-burden is now named as one plausible allocation heuristic among several (not asserted), while the paragraph’s actual thesis is narrowed to the weaker, less contestable claim that any allocation rule is only as good as the evidence feeding it — which is what the CRVS/NCoDV evidence in the rest of the paragraph actually supports.

title: CPHIA Conference Abstract (Draft)
text:
Suggested track

CONFIRMED (2026-09-24, from a user-supplied screenshot of the abstracts portal): the complete CPHIA 2026 track list is:

Elevating Africa as a leader in a reformed and inclusive global health architecture
Institutionalisation of Pandemic Prevention Preparedness & Response in Africa
African stakeholders’ empowerment and alignment to predictable, innovative and blended financing
Primary Health Care, digital transformation and AI-enabled health system
Unlocking opportunities for local manufacturing in Africa
Climate, health security, and African resilience

Recommended: Track 3 (“African stakeholders’ empowerment and alignment to predictable, innovative and blended financing”). This abstract’s actual content is about domestic financing decisions — whether the evidence used to justify health budget allocations is one African stakeholders (provincial DoH, National Treasury) actually own and engage with, or one anchored in externally-produced/uncorrected data by default — and its sharpest finding is precisely about which level of government is least empowered with the corrected-burden evidence that would make financing more defensible/predictable. That maps directly onto Track 3’s language, more so than any other track.
Track 1 (“reformed and inclusive global health architecture”) is the next-closest alternative — it echoes the conference’s overall sovereignty/ownership theme — but is framed around Africa’s role in global institutional reform, whereas this abstract stays entirely at the domestic financing-decision level; Track 3 is the better substantive fit. Tracks 2, 4, 5 and 6 do not match this abstract’s content and are not recommended.

title: CPHIA Conference Abstract (Draft)
section: Abstract body (~590 words — check against CPHIA’s actual word limit
text:
Abstract body (~590 words — check against CPHIA’s actual word limit
once confirmed; this draft now carries three decision-relevant findings (Stats SA vs. corrected-burden citation share, national vs. provincial; domestic vs. foreign corrected-burden estimates; and registered-mortality vs. corrected-burden vs. research/validation citation share over time) and will need trimming to fit)
Background. Whether health spending translates into better outcomes is itself a contested empirical question, already tested elsewhere in the South African literature. This project does not assume that spending should track disease burden in strict proportion — that is one plausible allocation heuristic among several, and reasonable people can disagree on how spending should be apportioned across need, cost-effectiveness, equity, or historical precedent. What is far less contestable is a narrower, prior claim: within a finite budget, some allocation decision is unavoidable, and whichever rule a government follows, that rule is only as good as the evidence used to inform it. Adjusted or corrected burden-of-disease estimates are not interchangeable with raw registered counts, which are susceptible to surveillance and reporting artefacts. South Africa’s civil registration and vital statistics (CRVS) system is a documented case of this risk: the SAMRC National Cause-of-Death Validation Project found only 36.9% agreement between officially registered and validated underlying cause of death across over 15,000 linked deaths, with a roughly four-to-one undercount of HIV/AIDS as underlying cause, substantial misclassification of injury deaths, and a high proportion of unusable codes. Two mechanisms plausibly drive these gaps: an unresolved tension between patient confidentiality and public health surveillance use of HIV-related death data, and non-specific (“ill-defined”) diagnoses written by certifying clinicians that central coders cannot reliably translate into ICD codes regardless of coder skill. If strategic planning documents anchor to registered (rather than corrected) burden estimates, whatever allocation rule they encode is being fed a distorted epidemiological signal — a risk concentrated in causes outside HIV/TB, including non-communicable diseases (NCDs) and violence/injury, which lack HIV/TB’s own dedicated correction model (Thembisa). This has not previously been empirically tested end-to-end against real provincial budget data.
Objectives. To build an open, reproducible pipeline that (1) assembles programme-level provincial health budget data, (2) traces which burden-of-disease data sources — both the global Global Burden of Disease (GBD) study and South Africa’s own SAMRC National Burden of Disease Study — are actually cited in the strategic planning documents that justify those budgets, and (3), in later work, quantifies the gap between registered and burden-corrected disease estimates as an input to a funding-gap analysis.
Methods. An AI-assisted extraction pipeline (R functions authored with AI coding-assistant support, run within an R {targets}-orchestrated pipeline) was built to fetch real, versioned provincial Health-department budget data (National Treasury’s Estimates of Provincial Revenue and Expenditure, “EPRE”) and to extract citations of known burden-of-disease data sources from National Department of Health strategic planning documents published over the last decade, using programmatic text search over the documents’ own published content. Citations were classified into three tracked evidence-source groups: registered mortality reporting (Stats SA’s own cause-of-death publications), corrected-burden estimates (the global GBD study and South Africa’s own SAMRC National Burden of Disease Study), and research/validation sources that could confirm or correct registered data’s accuracy (the SAMRC’s own National Cause-of-Death Validation study, Rapid Mortality Surveillance, and the Thembisa HIV model); citations of population-estimate/census sources were also identified but are not further dissected here. Citations of the health department’s own routine data/patient-monitoring systems (DHIS, TIER.net, EDRWeb) were tracked as a separate, fourth category throughout, so they never dilute the evidence-source counts above.
Preliminary results. A live pull of the 2024-25 EPRE release returned 42,578 real budget line items across all nine provinces (FY2020-FY2026) (see the Budget Panel chapter for the full interactive breakdown), confirming a consistent eight-programme provincial Health budget structure (see the Programme Crosswalk & Data Quality chapter for how raw programme-name variants were harmonised into that structure). A parallel extraction across six national strategic planning documents — three pre-2020 Annual Performance Plans (2017/18, 2018/19, 2019/20; the first of these covers the same fiscal year as the National Cause-of-Death Validation study’s own fieldwork) and three documents from 2020 onward (the 2020/21-2024/25 Strategic Plan, the 2025/26 Annual Performance Plan, and the 2025-2030 Strategic Plan) — found 122 citations of known burden-of-disease data sources (74 in the three pre-2020 documents, 48 in the three post-2020 documents), with Stats SA cited far more frequently (68/122) than either corrected-burden source: the Global Burden of Disease study (6/122) or the SAMRC’s own National Burden of Disease Study (5/122) — see the Citation Trail chapter for the full document-by-document, source-by-source breakdown behind every number in this paragraph. This is not a recent artefact: Stats SA’s share of citations is essentially unchanged across the pre-2020 and post-2020 document eras (52.7% vs. 60.4%; 39 of 74 pre-2020 citations vs. 29 of 48 post-2020). The two corrected-burden sources move in opposite directions over the same period: GBD’s share rose from 0% to 12.5% (0 of 74 pre-2020 citations vs. 6 of 48 post-2020), while the SAMRC National Burden of Disease Study’s share fell from 5.4% to 2.1% (4 of 74 vs. 1 of 48) — i.e. engagement with South Africa’s own domestically-produced corrected-burden estimate is shrinking even as engagement with a foreign corrected-burden estimate grows. Extending the citation trail to three provincial Annual Performance Plans (Gauteng, KwaZulu-Natal, Western Cape) — the sphere of government that actually sets EPRE allocations, not the National Department of Health — found these same sources cited less densely, and far more unevenly, than in national documents (39 citations in Gauteng’s APP vs. 14 and 13 in KwaZulu-Natal’s and Western Cape’s respectively), and found zero citations of the SAMRC National Burden of Disease Study in any of the three provincial documents. Reclassifying national citations into the three tracked groups above sharpens this picture further: registered-mortality citations are not being displaced by more corrected-burden or research/validation engagement over time — their own era share rose slightly (24.3% to 27.1%, pre- to post-2020 — 18 of 74 pre-2020 citations vs. 13 of 48 post-2020: a rising share of a shrinking pool) even as corrected-burden citations nearly tripled in share (5.4% to 14.6%; 4 of 74 vs. 7 of 48, GBD-driven), while research/validation citations — the ones that could actually justify trusting or correcting registered data — stayed essentially flat (8.1% to 8.3%; 6 of 74 vs. 4 of 48) and are carried almost entirely by Rapid Mortality Surveillance: the SAMRC’s own National Cause-of-Death Validation study, the source of this abstract’s own 36.9% validation estimate, has zero confirmed citations across all 9 documents sampled (see the Citation Trail chapter’s new registered-mortality-vs-corrected-burden-vs-research section for the full breakdown, including why this narrower “registered mortality” count is smaller than the raw “Stats SA” count above).
Conclusion. The decisions that translate disease burden into rand allocations are made mainly at provincial level, yet the planning documents that justify those decisions are anchored overwhelmingly in registered, uncorrected Stats SA statistics rather than either burden-corrected estimate — and provinces show even less consistent engagement with any of these sources than the National DoH does. A second, sharper finding sits inside that headline pattern: where corrected-burden evidence does appear, it is increasingly the global GBD estimate rather than South Africa’s own SAMRC National Burden of Disease Study, whose citation share is falling, not rising, and which is entirely absent from the three provincial documents sampled. For a conference organised around African health sovereignty, this is a concrete, quotable finding about what “ownership” of the evidence base for domestic health-financing decisions currently looks like in practice. Taken together with the two data-quality mechanisms above, this suggests two complementary, non-committal directions rather than a single fix: (1) giving domestically-produced corrected burden-of-disease estimates more visible standing in the documents that justify budgets, rather than defaulting to registered statistics or an externally-produced alternative, and (2) relocating ownership of diagnostic data quality to the certifying clinician who generates the diagnosis, since both confidentiality-driven under-recording and non-specific diagnoses originate at certification, not at central coding. A concrete next application of these data-quality deficits is a funding-gap analysis targeted at the causes shown above to be most exposed to registered-data distortion — non-communicable diseases (NCDs) and violence/injury-related spending — to investigate whether more efficient, proportional funding is possible once registered counts are replaced with corrected estimates. The more general, transferable point for other national and provincial policymakers is methodological rather than programmatic: before assuming that national or global burden-of-disease estimates are actually shaping local resource allocation, it is possible — and inexpensive — to check which sources are cited where the money is actually justified, using each jurisdiction’s own planning documents and data ecosystem rather than relying on any single external estimate. This case study demonstrates that check for South Africa; whether closing its own CRVS data-quality gaps needs investment precisely at the sphere of government shown here to be least engaged with burden-of-disease evidence is one of several questions it opens, for South Africa and potentially elsewhere.

Anticipated audience Q&A (prep notes, not part of the submitted abstract)
“Are these budgets funded by foreign aid or the local fiscus?” — likely given CPHIA’s health-financing-sovereignty framing. Every rand in this pipeline’s budget figures is domestic South African government expenditure (EPRE is a Treasury/provincial-legislature document, not a donor ledger); we have not yet split that into equitable-share vs. conditional-grant portions, and true foreign donor financing (PEPFAR, Global Fund) sits structurally outside this dataset. The ~10.6–10.8% domestic-only HIV/TB budget share (see the Descriptive Statistics chapter) is a floor, not the full picture — donor-vs-domestic decomposition is an explicit, not-yet-started next step (see the Plan & Open Questions chapter’s “Future / related projects” section), not something answered with unwarranted certainty here.

title: Plan & Open Questions
section: Why CRVS data quality is weak (mechanisms, not this project’s own finding)
text:
Why CRVS data quality is weak (mechanisms, not this project’s own finding)
Two mechanisms documented in the general CRVS/ICD-coding literature plausibly explain the NCoDV gap (see Overview chapter): (1) an unresolved tension between patient confidentiality and public health surveillance use of HIV-related death data, which plausibly drives under-recording of HIV/AIDS as underlying cause; and (2) non-specific (“ill-defined”) diagnoses written by the certifying clinician, which central ICD coders cannot reliably translate into a specific code regardless of coder skill. Neither mechanism has been tested against this project’s own data — they motivate the two candidate, non-committal recommendation directions below, not a demonstrated result.
Preliminary, non-committal recommendation directions (pending the funding-gap analysis, steps 2-3 above):

Better representation of local burden-of-disease estimates — give domestically-produced corrected estimates (the SAMRC’s own National Burden of Disease Study) more visible standing in the documents that justify budgets, rather than defaulting to registered statistics or an externally-produced alternative (GBD).
Ownership of data quality by the data generator — relocate responsibility for diagnostic data quality to the certifying clinician who writes the diagnosis, since both confidentiality-driven under-recording and non-specific diagnoses originate at certification, not at central coding.

title: Plan & Open Questions
section: Second-pass review: CRVS, policy and systems lens (planned, not findings)
text:
Second-pass review: CRVS, policy and systems lens (planned, not findings)
This expert review (2026-10-21) found five design gaps. The full plan and its sequencing are in docs/PLAN.md.

The exposure is unmeasured. No CRVS quality metric exists yet. The plan is a province × year panel (% ill-defined/garbage codes, completeness, timeliness) built on established frameworks (VSPI, ANACONDA).
The channels are unspecified. Provincial budgets are organised by service platform, not by disease. Burden data most plausibly reaches allocation through the risk adjustment in the provincial equitable-share formula. A counterfactual re-run of that formula with registered vs. corrected burden is the most specific feasible test.
The discretionary margin is small. Compensation of employees is about 64% of FY2024 provincial health appropriations (ad hoc check, not yet in the pipeline). Any effect should be sought in increments and non-personnel lines.
Only differential error matters. Uniform under-registration leaves cause shares unchanged. Only misclassification that differs across causes or provinces can distort relative allocation.
Citation is not use. Citation function (instrumental, conceptual, symbolic) will be coded with an inter-rater reliability check, and “funding gap” is renamed a descriptive burden–allocation divergence.

title: Plan & Open Questions
section: Future / related projects (out of scope for this thesis)
text:
Future / related projects (out of scope for this thesis)
Scaffold only, not started. A mirror-image companion study asking, for the HIV/TB population this thesis deliberately excludes (see Hypothesis above), whether the dedicated Thembisa epidemiological model is actually cited and correctly drives budget advocacy, and where that budget actually comes from (domestic fiscus vs. PEPFAR/Global Fund donor funding). HIV/TB is excluded from the main funding-gap analysis because it already has a dedicated, purpose-built epidemiological model rather than relying on registered/corrected mortality data the way other causes do — this project asks whether that model’s existence actually translates into well-calibrated budget advocacy, or is cited only nominally.
Draft research questions:

Citation frequency — how often, and in what form, is Thembisa actually cited in South African HIV/TB strategic planning documents (the national HIV/TB/STI NSP, conditional grant business plans, provincial HIV/TB APPs)? (citation_source_patterns in R/extract_app_citations.R already has a working thembisa regex — update (2026-09-24): it returned exactly 1 match across the current 9-document registry (Western Cape’s 2025/26 APP, p59), but none of those 9 documents are HIV/TB-specific — this question is about HIV/TB-dedicated planning documents specifically, still not yet sampled. See the Citation Trail chapter’s registered-mortality-vs-corrected-burden-vs-research section, where Thembisa is one of three tracked research/validation sources.)
Advocacy accuracy — where Thembisa is cited, do the corresponding budget requests/targets actually track its modelled outputs (projected people on ART, new infections, TB incidence/treatment targets), or is it cited as background while budget figures are driven by something else (historical allocation, flat-rate escalation)?
Funding provenance — regardless of (1)-(2), where does HIV/TB budget actually come from (domestic fiscus vs. PEPFAR/Global Fund), and how has that mix shifted given the 2025 PEPFAR/USAID funding disruptions reported in the South African HIV sector?

A prime candidate document is already known and verified: SANAC’s National Strategic Plan on HIV, TB and STIs 2017-2022 (found, downloaded, and confirmed via pdftotext during the main thesis’s pre-2020 citation hunt, then excluded from the main registry as out-of-scope — wrong organisation, disease-specific). Its current-edition successor would need to be located at sanac.org.za (not yet checked). Other not-yet-fetched sources needed: HIV/TB conditional grant business plans (Division of Revenue Act annexes), PEPFAR South Africa Country Operational Plan documents, and Global Fund grant/disbursement data for South Africa.
If started, this should get its own registry/scripts (reusing the existing extract_source_citations()/build_citation_trail() functions rather than duplicating them) and its own PLAN/KNOWLEDGE-style register, kept separate from the main thesis so a positive-control or sustainability finding here doesn’t get blended with the main CRVS argument.

title: Programme Crosswalk & Data Quality
text:
Real provincial EPRE data uses province-specific spelling variants for the same underlying budget programme — for example “Health Sciences and Training” is also rendered “Health Science & Training” (Free State) and “Health Science and Training” (North West); “Emergency Medical Services” is rendered with a double space in KwaZulu-Natal, and as “EMERGENCY MADICAL SERVICES” (an apparent typo) in Limpopo.
R/crosswalk_programmes.R’s normalise_programme_name() resolves these via whitespace/punctuation cleanup plus a small-edit-distance fuzzy match against the canonical eight-programme list, and every decision is logged for audit.

title: Citation Trail
text:
R/extract_app_citations.R downloads real National Department of Health strategic documents (Annual Performance Plan, Strategic Plans), and, since this update, 3 provincial Departments of Health’s Annual Performance Plans (Gauteng, KwaZulu-Natal, Western Cape), and searches their text for mentions of known burden-of-disease evidence sources: Stats SA, Global Burden of Disease (GBD), the SAMRC’s own National Burden of Disease Study (added 2026-09-23 — distinct from both GBD and the SAMRC’s separate NCoDV registration-validation study), SADHS, GHS, District Health Barometer, NCoDV, Rapid Mortality Surveillance, and Thembisa — plus, since a later 2026 update, mentions of NDoH’s own internal routine data systems (EDRWeb, TIER.net, DHIS, NICD), tracked as a separate source_category so they never dilute an evidence-source percentage (see “NDoH’s own routine data systems” below).
A live run across 9 confirmed documents (6 national + 3 provincial) found 188 evidence-source citation matches (plus 132 routine-data-system matches, see below) — 3 live (2020+) national documents (2020/21-2024/25 Strategic Plan, 2025/26 Annual Performance Plan, 2025-2030 Strategic Plan — only 2 distinct document years, 2020 and 2025, since two of the three are both dated 2025), 3 archived pre-2020 national Annual Performance Plans (2017/18-2019/20, 2018/19-2020/21, 2019/20-2021/22 — 3 distinct document years, one per document) found via the Internet Archive Wayback Machine (the live health.gov.za site was migrated to a new CMS and no longer serves pre-2020 documents), and 3 live provincial Annual Performance Plans found via targeted DuckDuckGo searches and individually curl-verified. The pre-2020 APPs extend coverage before COVID-19 and, critically, the 2017/18-2019/20 APP covers the exact fiscal year the NCoDV validation study’s fieldwork was conducted in. Stats SA is by far the most frequently cited source in both spheres — and provincial documents cite it even more heavily, proportionally, than national ones (see the national-vs-provincial chart below). Only 3 of 9 provinces are covered so far (see Still open).

Provincial extension: partially done. 3 of 9 provinces (Gauteng, KwaZulu-Natal, Western Cape — the 3 largest by population and Health budget share) are now in the registry, confirmed via targeted DuckDuckGo searches and individually curl-verified before being added (never guessed). The remaining 6 provinces’ APP/Strategic Plan URLs are not yet confirmed. Matches are still whole-source mentions, not yet tied to a specific cited report year or budget line. Regex matching counts textual mentions, not verified data usage — a document could name a source once and still base its actual targets on a different, unmatched source. Raw per-document counts are also not length-normalized (the longest document, ndoh_app_2017_18_2019_20, has more total pages, not unusually dense citation per page).
Pre-2020 extension: done. The document registry previously started at the 2020/21-2024/25 Strategic Plan; it now also includes 3 real archived Annual Performance Plans (2017/18-2019/20, 2018/19-2020/21, 2019/20-2021/22), each confirmed via the Wayback Machine and verified by downloading and checking the actual title page before being registered. This grew the citation-event sample from 47 to 122 national matches (188 total including provincial, after also adding the SAMRC National Burden of Disease Study pattern on 2026-09-23) and, for the first time, gives citation-trail coverage of the exact 2017/18 fiscal year the NCoDV validation study’s fieldwork was conducted in. Two candidate documents were investigated and ruled out as out of scope (a disease-specific Malaria Elimination Strategic Plan, and SANAC’s HIV/TB/STI National Strategic Plan — a different organisation, not NDoH); two further candidates had corrupted/truncated Wayback captures and were unusable. See docs/KNOWLEDGE.md for full detail. This citation-mix evidence (how heavily registered vs. burden-corrected sources are cited, and whether that holds at the provincial level where budgets are actually set) remains the project’s strongest starting point for motivating a CRVS data-quality assessment.

title: Overview
text: Does the quality (completeness, timeliness, diagnostic accuracy) of South Africa’s civil registration and vital statistics (CRVS) data distort how health resource allocation is calibrated across programmes, particularly for causes outside HIV/TB (which are modelled separately via the Thembisa epidemiological model and are out of scope here)? This question has not been answered by this project yet.

title: Overview
text: Does the quality (completeness, timeliness, diagnostic accuracy) of South Africa’s civil registration and vital statistics (CRVS) data distort how health resource allocation is calibrated across programmes, particularly for causes outside HIV/TB (which are modelled separately via the Thembisa epidemiological model and are out of scope here)? This question has not been answered by this project yet.

title: Overview
text:
Working hypothesis
CRVS data-quality issues — incomplete registration, delayed reporting, diagnostic misclassification of underlying cause of death — may distort how provincial and national health budgets are allocated across programmes. This is the question this pipeline is built to investigate, not a conclusion already reached. It is distinct from existing South African literature that asks whether health spending affects outcomes directly: this project sits upstream of that question, asking whether the spending itself is calibrated against burden estimates already known to be wrong.
Two mechanisms documented in the general CRVS/ICD-coding literature plausibly explain part of this data-quality gap (not yet tested against this project’s own data): an unresolved tension between patient confidentiality and public health surveillance use of HIV-related death data, and non-specific (“ill-defined”) diagnoses written by certifying clinicians that central coders cannot reliably translate into ICD codes regardless of coder skill — see the Plan & Open Questions chapter for the two preliminary, non-committal recommendation directions these mechanisms suggest.

title: Cross-Country Landscape
text:
Note



Status: all planned countries populated, now with annual-series trend data. This chapter extends the South-Africa-only citation trail (see Citation Trail) to other Bloomberg Philanthropies Data for Health (D4H) Initiative countries, using the same method: search each country’s own national health budgets/policies/ strategic plans for mentions of known burden-of-disease evidence sources — now generalised into a single, cross-country evidence-category taxonomy (see evidence_category_taxonomy in R/constants.R). A second pass (documented in docs/PLAN.md) added annual/recurring publication series for each of the 7 new countries — Uganda’s Annual Health Sector Performance Report, India’s National Health Profile, Rwanda’s annual performance reports, Morocco’s “Santé en Chiffres”, Zambia’s Joint Annual Review, and a Thailand statistics edition — so every country now has >=3 documents spanning several years, enabling a year-over-year trend view below, not just a single snapshot. A follow-up pass also split a new local_surveillance_system evidence category out of the general routine-data-system bucket — named disease- surveillance systems and their own reported counts (e.g. Integrated Disease Surveillance and Response/IDSR, sentinel surveillance) are a genuine evidence product, distinct from general-purpose HMIS/DHIS2 infrastructure. A third pass added real national/health budget documents for the first time — Morocco’s Finance Bill macro/execution report, Rwanda’s Budget Speech and a UNICEF Health Budget Brief, India’s “Demand No. 46” (the Ministry of Health’s own Union Budget appropriation chapter, 3 editions), Kenya’s Programme Based Budget, and Thailand’s Budget in Brief — tagged document_type health_budget/national_budget. A fourth pass specifically re-checked known document sources for missing in-between years: India’s National Health Profile series now runs every year 2018-2023 (2019/2021/2022 added), and Morocco’s “Santé en Chiffres” gained a 2021 edition — both confirmed real, official-domain documents. 52 documents, 8 countries, 1,966 total citation matches (1,490 evidence-source + 476 routine-data-system) — confirmed real document URLs, curl + title-page verified — see docs/KNOWLEDGE.md. This chapter is a landscape view: it does not replicate South Africa’s full numeric budget-panel analysis for these countries, only the document/citation inventory.

Trend findings (still a small sample per country-year, treat as pointers not conclusions): population_estimate (census/DHS-family surveys) is the dominant category in almost every country-year, with no consistent rise or fall over time within any single country — unlike South Africa’s own GBD share, which rose from 0% (pre-2020) to 12.5% (post-2020) in the existing era comparison. The annual-series documents surfaced three categories the original 2-document snapshot had entirely missed for specific countries: Uganda’s AHSPR editions are the first Uganda documents to name a local_epidemiological_model (the UNAIDS Spectrum tool, narrowly pattern-matched to avoid “autism spectrum disorders” false positives) and the first to show Uganda citing GBD; Rwanda’s two annual reports are the first Rwanda documents with a verbal_autopsy citation (and with 7 matches, the richest verbal-autopsy example in the whole project); and India’s National Health Profile editions are the first India documents citing the decennial Population Census as a named demographic source, alongside a new other-category National Health Accounts citation (also newly found in Uganda and Rwanda). Both Uganda and India’s annual-series documents also reveal heavy reliance on their own routine health-information systems (bare DHIS2/HMIS) — tagged routine_data_system, not evidence_source, consistent with how South Africa’s DHIS/NICD and Kenya’s KHIS/KEMRI are already treated. Separately, a named- surveillance-system category (local_surveillance_system) was split out for 5 countries once IDSR/sentinel-surveillance mentions were checked in context: Uganda (35 matches), India (25), Rwanda (12), Kenya (10), and Zambia (2) all genuinely cite a specific surveillance system or its own reports (e.g. Kenya’s “Weekly IDSR reports are produced on notifiable conditions”) as evidence — not the same as citing bare HMIS/DHIS2 infrastructure, so these are kept as their own evidence category rather than folded into the routine/NA bucket.

title: Cross-Country Landscape
text:
Evidence-category mix, by country
Each country’s own total evidence-source citation matches are treated as 100% here, so this compares which evidence categories dominate each country’s own citation practice — not the absolute number of matches, which depends heavily on how many documents/pages are sampled for each country so far (South Africa: 9 documents; India: 8; Morocco: 6; Rwanda: 6; Uganda: 6; Kenya: 5; Thailand: 4; Zambia: 4).












Note



So what: early, small-sample findings (2 documents per country, 4 for Kenya — not yet enough to generalise, but notable):

Zambia’s 2017 and 2022 national strategic plans both name a specific local epidemiological model by name — “Spectrum” (the UNAIDS/Avenir Health HIV demographic-projection tool) — the same role South Africa’s Thembisa model plays, but for a different country’s own HIV programme. Every other country sampled (Rwanda, Thailand, Uganda, India, Kenya) either doesn’t name an equivalent model, or uses the word “spectrum”/“model” only in an unrelated generic sense (“broad-spectrum antibiotics”, “full spectrum of health services”, “across the health spectrum”, management-consulting frameworks like the McKinsey 7S Model) — confirmed independently for Rwanda, India, and Kenya by inspecting each match’s actual context before excluding it, not assumed; the same false positive recurring across three unrelated countries is itself notable.
Three independent countries now have a real named verbal_autopsy citation: Zambia’s 2022-2026 plan (“Sample Vital Registration with Verbal Autopsy”, SAVVY), India’s National Health Mission framework (“verbal autopsy at community level”), and Kenya’s 2018-2023 KHSSP (a costed verbal-autopsy plan integrated into its CRVS system) — the new verbal_autopsy evidence category this cross-country extension added to the original South-Africa-only taxonomy now has three independent real examples.
Kenya’s 2023-2027 KHSSP produced the project’s first real hdss_site citation: a mention that the Kenya Biovax Institute “continues to manage Health and Demographic Surveillance Systems (HDSS) targeting population dynamics.” A modest first example (1 match, no specific site named) rather than a rich one — but real, confirmed by context, not pattern-matched on a false positive. Notably, “Kilifi” (the real KEMRI-Wellcome Trust HDSS site’s home county) appears repeatedly across all 4 Kenya documents, but every instance checked is an ordinary county-name mention (stunting/coverage tables) — not a reference to that research site — so no pattern was built on the county name itself.
A real cross-country false-positive risk was caught and fixed repeatedly: Rwanda’s “RBC” (Rwanda Biomedical Centre) collides with unrelated “RBC” (Red Blood Cell) text in Zambia’s own document; Thailand’s own “DHS” (district health system) is unrelated to the Demographic and Health Survey acronym used by Zambia/Rwanda/Uganda; and Kenya’s “Kilifi” county-name mentions are unrelated to its own real HDSS site of the same name — all three handled by scoping each country’s patterns to its own documents only (see R/extract_app_citations.R’s country filter) and by checking every match’s context before writing a pattern, not a single shared acronym list applied blindly.

Second-pass addendum (annual-series extension): findings 1 and 2 above are no longer unique to Zambia/Zambia+India+Kenya once the annual-series documents are included — see the “Trend findings” callout above for the updated counts (Uganda now also has a local_epidemiological_model and a GBD citation; Rwanda now also has verbal_autopsy, its richest example in the project). Finding 3 (Kenya’s hdss_site) and the Kilifi false-positive catch in finding 4 are unchanged by the new documents. A further follow-up split a new local_surveillance_system category (IDSR/sentinel surveillance) out of the routine-data-system bucket for Uganda, India, Rwanda, Zambia and Kenya — see the “Trend findings” callout above.

title: Cross-Country Landscape
text:
Still open

All 8 countries now have >=3 documents spanning several years (South Africa: 9, 2017-2025; Uganda: 6, 2014-2025; India: 5, 2012-2023; Morocco: 5, 2012-2024; Rwanda: 4, 2012-2024; Zambia: 4, 2011-2022; Kenya: 4, 2013-2023; Thailand: 3, 2017-2024) — a real improvement over the original 2-document snapshot per new country, but still a small sample for generalising beyond “this specific set of documents”; Thailand and Zambia’s annual series are thinner than the other 6 countries’ (see below), a genuine data-availability limit, not a search-effort shortfall.
Three documents still genuinely cite zero matched evidence sources under the current patterns — confirmed by directly checking which document each keyword match actually came from, not assumed: Thailand’s 17th National Health Assembly resolution and Morocco’s “Plan Santé 2025” executive-summary deck (both short policy/summary documents, not a pattern-coverage gap); and Uganda’s Health Service Commission Strategic Plan 2020-2025 (its patterns only matched Uganda’s other documents). India’s National Health Policy 2017, previously zero, now has matches picked up by the second-pass india_census/india_nha patterns.
Uganda’s official Ministry of Health Strategic Plan 2020/21-2024/25 is a confirmed real document, but was not registrable this round: its official host (library.health.go.ug) refused the TLS connection outright, and its WHO-hosted mirror downloaded but failed to parse (corrupted PDF) — both ruled out rather than silently substituted; the two Uganda strategic documents actually used (Health Service Commission Strategic Plan, National Health Compact) are real alternates, not the first choice.
Rwanda’s FY2021-22 Annual Health Sector Performance Report was attempted for the annual-series extension but dropped: its official mirror downloaded as a valid, complete PDF but is genuinely corrupted server-side (unrecoverable even after qpdf repair), and the alternate Joint Sector Review mirror found for the same year turned out to be a scanned image PDF with zero extractable text — both ruled out rather than silently substituted with a weaker proxy.
Thailand and Zambia’s annual-series searches hit genuine data-availability limits: only 1 additional English-readable Thailand statistics edition could be found (search returned “no more results” after 2 rounds), and only 2 additional Zambia Joint Annual Review editions (2011, 2012) could be found, with no editions located between 2012 and the existing 2017 strategic plan.
A fourth pass (2026-10-14) specifically re-checked all 7 new countries’ known document sources for missing in-between years. India’s National Health Profile gap closed completely (2019/2021/2022 found, all official domain — the series now runs every year 2018-2023) and Morocco’s “Santé en Chiffres” gained a 2021 edition (also official domain), narrowing its gap to just 2022-2023. Uganda’s AHSPR FY2023/24 edition, Rwanda’s missing 2013-2017/2021-2022 annual reports, Zambia’s missing 2013-2016/2018-2021 JAR editions, and Morocco’s 2022-2023 Santé en Chiffres editions were all re-searched but not found as direct, workable PDF links — genuine, re-confirmed data-availability gaps (strategic plans like Kenya’s and Zambia’s KHSSP/NHSP are legitimately multi-year documents by design, not a search gap; the AHSPR/NHP/JAR/Santé-en-Chiffres annual series genuinely should exist for every year but aren’t all web-accessible). library.health.go.ug (Uganda’s official MoH document host) was re-tested and remains unreachable (connection refused), consistent with earlier findings.
No subnational documents for the new countries yet (national-level only, per the confirmed scope for this phase — see docs/PLAN.md).
Real national/health budget documents are now registered for 5 of 7 new countries (Morocco, Rwanda, India, Kenya, Thailand) — still only as document_type metadata for the citation trail, per docs/PLAN.md’s “Budget depth” decision, not parsed for numeric amounts like South Africa’s EPRE panel. Three of these 5 countries’ budget documents (Morocco’s PLF, Rwanda’s Budget Speech, and all 3 editions of India’s Demand No. 46) genuinely cite zero evidence sources — confirmed by inspecting their full extracted text, consistent with being pure financial/establishment-table documents rather than health-sector narratives. No budget document could be found for Uganda (only an Office-of-the-Prime-Minister vote estimate was found, not the Health vote specifically) or Zambia — genuine data-availability gaps, documented rather than forced.
All 8 planned D4H countries are now populated with annual-series trend data — the IHEA 2027 World Congress abstract chapter has been updated with the new headline numbers (see docs/PLAN.md).

title: Budget Panel
text:
Descriptive statistics & policy framing
A fuller descriptive-statistics pass over this same real data — budget size/growth, provincial distribution, economic-classification and programme composition, the HIV/AIDS+TB subprogramme base rate, and a grounded answer to the anticipated CPHIA “foreign aid vs. local fiscus” question — is browsable as tabbed tables/charts in the Descriptive Statistics chapter (Rscript scripts/run_budget_descriptive_stats.R to reproduce the underlying CSVs). Headline points:

~93% of the Health budget is “Current payments” (staff/goods & services) in both FY2023 and FY2024, leaving under 5% as a capital envelope — any new infrastructure ask (including CRVS-adjacent data-systems asks) competes for a small, largely pre-committed slice.
District Health Services is both the single largest programme (~47%) and the one closest to facility-level mortality/notification data — the natural home for a CRVS-data-quality argument aimed at provincial Health budgets.
HIV/AIDS + TB subprogrammes account for ~10.6-10.8% of the provincial Health budget (R27.4bn in FY2024) — a real base rate for the excluded population this thesis deliberately doesn’t analyse (see the Plan & Open Questions chapter’s “Future / related projects” section), and it is entirely domestic-government money as far as this dataset can see (EPRE does not capture foreign donor financing at all — see the Descriptive Statistics chapter for the full sovereignty/foreign-aid framing).
